en: The Philippine tarsier has enormous eyes that are actually larger than its brain, helping it hunt insects in the dark forests of Bohol.
The Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park in the Sulu Sea protects over 600 species of fish and 360 species of hard corals.
The Tamaraw, a small hoofed mammal related to the water buffalo, is critically endangered and found only in the mountainous forests of Mindoro.
The Aedes aegypti mosquito spreads dengue fever when it bites humans, and it lays its eggs in the clean, stagnant water found in tires or pots.
The Philippine pitcher plant, locally called kobukobong, traps and digests insects using slippery, pitcher-shaped leaves to survive in nutrient-poor mountain soils.
The Philippine eagle has a distinctive shaggy crest of brown feathers and powerful talons to hunt monkeys and flying lemurs in the canopy.
Eating calamansi, a native Philippine citrus fruit, provides vitamin C which helps the human body produce collagen and fight off infections.
Mangrove trees in Palawan grow specialized aerial roots called pneumatophores that stick up from the mud to absorb oxygen during high tide.
The rice plant, or palay, grows from a germinated seed into a mature stalk that produces grain-filled panicles in flooded fields.
Butanding, or whale sharks, migrate to the warm coastal waters of Donsol, Sorsogon every year to feed on tiny plankton.
Philippine carabaos wallow in mud to cool their bodies and protect their skin from the sun because they lack functional sweat glands.
Abaca, a species of banana plant native to the Philippines, is harvested for its strong fibers used to make Manila rope.
